Can somebody explain to me what IP addresses are and how they affect our computers.

Computers on the internet work by sending data to each other, which is split up into small fragments called packets. For example, when you want to load a website, your computer sends data containing a request to a web server, which responds with the web page you requested.

These packets are sent through a number of intermediate points in the internet called routers. So if your computer sends a request to a web server, how do these routers know where they should deliver it? The answer is that this web server (and indeed every computer connected to the internet) has been assigned an IP address, which uniquely identifies it in the network. Each router can work out where to forward the packets next based on the IP address it is being sent to.

Similarly, when the server sends your web page back as a response, it needs to know the IP address from which it was sent, so it can be delivered to the right computer. Each packet has a source and a destination IP address.

When you type a URL into your web browser, the name (such as voat.co) is translated into an IP address, which looks something like 108.162.201.136. This is how your computer knows where to send the packet.

In reality, not every computer has its own unique IP address. For example you are most likely sharing a home network with other users or devices, and your router has a public-facing IP address that is shared by all users in your network.

This is a very high-level overview with a lot of simplifications and omissions, so please ask if you have any questions or don't understand anything!

(Also I'm no expert, so if I have any misconceptions in my explanation someone please point them out!)

I actually popped in because I figured I'd need to add the point about subnets (while I'm not a specialist, I am an expert), but since it's already here I'll add one more thing: the way IP addresses are assigned is also done in a relatively systematic way that helps things get routed effectively. You can think of it sort of like area codes, except that rather than being mapped to areas things map to "subnets" of interconnected computers (or devices with multiple computers behind them) which would all have IP addresses like 108.162.201.1XX. For example, here's an XKCD that gives a rough map of the first XXX block as of 2006. This means that while you can't necessarily know where the physical computer is, it's relatively easy to figure out where to send your traffic so that it'll get where it's going: you can tell whether it's local traffic (so long as you know what your subnet is), or whether it needs to be forwarded out and in what general direction.

Think of an IP address as a phone number for your computer. Just as everyone has to have a unique phone number, you wouldn't want to call your mother and connect to a gas station in Botswana, every device that connects to the Internet also requires a unique IP address to establish communication between them. (Since this is ELI5 I am not going into NAT/PAT and other methods to have multiple devices with the same IP).

In order to make that into something easy for people to understand, DNS is used. That is what translates the IP address into a name, for instance instead of having to remember 74.125.21.100 you can type in google.com in your browser.
